The optical device is configured to stabilize images by using two deformable optical elements: a first deformable membrane and a second deformable membrane. These membranes are arranged so that their deformation can modify the optical behavior of the device, for example by compensating for movement, vibration, or tilt that would otherwise degrade image quality.

Each of the deformable membranes is connected to a support structure by a respective peripheral anchoring area. This anchoring area extends around the membrane and fixes the membrane to the support while allowing at least a central portion of the membrane to deform during operation. In this way, each membrane remains mechanically held in position while still being capable of controlled displacement or shape modification.

A constant volume of fluid is enclosed between the first deformable membrane and the second deformable membrane. This fluid mechanically couples the two membranes to one another. As a result, deformation of one membrane can influence the shape or position of the other membrane through the incompressible or substantially incompressible fluid volume. The constant volume of fluid allows the two membranes to cooperate in producing a desired optical effect while maintaining a stable internal mechanical relationship.

The optical device further includes actuation devices associated with each membrane. These actuation devices are arranged to act on regions of the membranes located between the respective peripheral anchoring area and the central part of each membrane. The actuation devices for the first membrane and the actuation devices for the second membrane are separate, so that the deformation of each membrane can be controlled independently or in a coordinated manner. By applying forces to these intermediate membrane regions, the device can adjust the curvature, inclination, or local displacement of the membranes without directly actuating only the central optical area.

A control means is provided to operate the actuation devices. The control means is configured to apply actuation voltages to the actuation devices starting from a rest position of the membranes. By selectively controlling these voltages, the control means can operate the device in multiple modes. These modes may include, for example, coordinated deformation of the two membranes, differential deformation between the membranes, or selective actuation of particular membrane regions to compensate for image motion. Through this controlled actuation, the optical device provides image stabilization while preserving the mechanical coupling produced by the constant fluid volume between the two deformable membranes.
outputs.L4:
An optical image stabilization device includes a deformable optical element formed from two flexible membranes that are mechanically coupled to one another through a substantially constant volume of fluid. Each membrane is secured at an outer peripheral or anchored edge and includes a central region that can deform in response to mechanical forces. Because the two membranes are connected by the enclosed fluid volume, deformation of one membrane produces a corresponding pressure change in the fluid, which can influence the shape or position of the other membrane. This arrangement allows the optical properties of the device, such as beam direction, focal behavior, or image position, to be adjusted without requiring large mechanical translation of a conventional lens element.

The device further includes separate actuators associated with the respective membranes. A first actuator is positioned between the anchored edge and the central region of the first membrane, while a second actuator is positioned between the anchored edge and the central region of the second membrane. Each actuator may be configured to apply a controllable force to its corresponding membrane when an electrical voltage is supplied. For example, the actuators may be piezoelectric, electrostatic, electromagnetic, or otherwise electrically driven elements capable of producing localized membrane deformation. By placing the actuators between the fixed edge and the deformable central region, the device can efficiently control the curvature, tilt, or displacement of the membranes.

A control system is connected to the actuators and is configured to selectively apply voltages to one or both actuators. The control system may receive input signals from motion sensors, image sensors, gyroscopes, accelerometers, or other detection components that identify unwanted movement of the imaging system. Based on these signals, the control system determines the appropriate actuator response needed to compensate for the detected motion. The control system may operate in multiple modes, including a mode in which voltage is applied primarily to the first actuator, a mode in which voltage is applied primarily to the second actuator, and a mode in which both actuators are driven together or in a coordinated manner.

When voltage is applied to one actuator, the corresponding membrane deforms, changing the pressure distribution within the constant fluid volume. This pressure change can cause the opposite membrane to deform in a complementary way. When voltage is applied to both actuators, the membranes can be shaped more precisely, allowing the optical element to produce a desired stabilizing effect. By adjusting the relative voltages applied to the actuators, the device can control the membrane deformation dynamically and continuously.

In operation, the optical image stabilization device compensates for hand shake, vibration, or other unintended movement that could otherwise blur an image. The deformable membranes alter the optical path of incoming light so that the image remains substantially stable on an image sensor or within an optical system. Because stabilization is achieved through controlled membrane deformation rather than by moving a large lens assembly, the device can be compact, lightweight, and energy efficient. This makes it suitable for use in cameras, mobile devices, medical imaging systems, optical instruments, and other applications where precise image stabilization is desired.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in meaning and clarity. It is called a definite article, and it helps identify a specific person, place, thing, or idea. For example, when we say “the book,” we are talking about a particular book, not just any book.

Although “the” is short and simple, it gives sentences structure and precision. It can point to something already mentioned, something unique, or something understood by both the speaker and the listener. Phrases like “the sun,” “the world,” and “the answer” all rely on this small word to create clear meaning.

In many ways, “the” shows how even the smallest words can have great importance. Without it, English would sound less natural and often less clear. This tiny word proves that language is built not only from big, expressive terms, but also from small words that quietly hold everything together.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an invention in formal patent language: an optical device with first and second deformable membranes, a support anchoring their peripheries, enclosed fluid for mechanical coupling, and voltage-controlled actuation devices with multiple operating modes.
counterfactuals.output:
An optical device is disclosed comprising a fluidically coupled, voltage-actuated deformable optical element. The device includes a support structure defining an optical aperture and anchoring respective peripheral portions of a first deformable membrane and a second deformable membrane. The first and second deformable membranes are disposed in spaced relation so as to at least partially bound an enclosed chamber containing a substantially incompressible optical fluid. Deformation of one of the membranes causes displacement of the optical fluid and corresponding deformation of the other membrane, thereby providing mechanical coupling between the membranes through the enclosed fluid.

The optical device further comprises one or more voltage-controlled actuation devices operatively associated with at least one of the first and second deformable membranes. The actuation devices are configured to apply controllable forces to selected regions of the associated membrane in response to one or more electrical drive signals. The optical device is operable in a plurality of operating modes, including a first mode in which the first and second membranes deform cooperatively to vary an optical power of the device, a second mode in which differential deformation of the membranes produces a change in an optical aberration characteristic, and a third mode in which the membranes are maintained in a selected configuration to provide a predetermined optical state.

In one embodiment, the first deformable membrane defines a first optically transmissive surface and the second deformable membrane defines a second optically transmissive surface. The enclosed fluid has a refractive index selected relative to surrounding media such that changes in curvature of one or both membranes alter an optical path of light passing through the optical aperture. The support structure may comprise a substantially rigid annular frame, spacer, or housing member configured to maintain a fixed peripheral spacing between the membranes while permitting central portions thereof to deform.

The voltage-controlled actuation devices may comprise electrostatic, piezoelectric, dielectric elastomer, electromagnetic, or electroactive polymer actuators, or combinations thereof. In certain implementations, the actuation devices include a plurality of individually addressable electrodes disposed about the optical aperture, whereby spatially selective membrane deformation is achieved by applying respective voltages to the electrodes. A controller may be coupled to the actuation devices and configured to generate drive signals corresponding to selected optical functions, including focus adjustment, astigmatism correction, spherical aberration correction, beam steering, wavefront shaping, optical image stabilization, or combinations thereof.

In operation, application of a first voltage pattern to the actuation devices produces a substantially axisymmetric displacement of at least one membrane, thereby changing the focal length of the optical device. Application of a second voltage pattern produces a non-axisymmetric displacement profile, thereby modifying an aberration or steering an optical wavefront. Application of a third voltage pattern maintains the optical device in a latched, biased, or neutral optical configuration. The fluid coupling between the first and second membranes distributes mechanical pressure within the chamber and enables controlled, repeatable deformation of the membranes in response to the voltage-controlled actuation.

In claim-style form, the invention may be characterized as follows:

1. An optical device comprising:  
   a support structure defining an optical aperture;  
   a first deformable membrane having a peripheral portion anchored to the support structure;  
   a second deformable membrane spaced from the first deformable membrane and having a peripheral portion anchored to the support structure;  
   an enclosed volume disposed between the first and second deformable membranes and containing an optical fluid, the optical fluid mechanically coupling deformation of the first deformable membrane to deformation of the second deformable membrane; and  
   at least one voltage-controlled actuation device configured to deform at least one of the first and second deformable membranes in response to an applied voltage,  
   wherein the optical device is selectively operable in a plurality of operating modes to vary an optical characteristic of light transmitted through the optical aperture.

2. The optical device of claim 1, wherein the plurality of operating modes comprise at least two of: a variable-focus mode, an aberration-correction mode, a beam-steering mode, a wavefront-shaping mode, and an optical-stabilization mode.

3. The optical device of claim 1, wherein the at least one voltage-controlled actuation device comprises a plurality of independently addressable actuator elements arranged circumferentially around the optical aperture.

4. The optical device of claim 3, wherein the independently addressable actuator elements are configured to generate axisymmetric and non-axisymmetric deformation profiles of at least one of the first and second deformable membranes.

5. The optical device of claim 1, wherein the optical fluid is substantially incompressible and optically transmissive.

6. The optical device of claim 1, further comprising a controller configured to apply different voltage patterns to the at least one voltage-controlled actuation device to select among the plurality of operating modes.

7. The optical device of claim 1, wherein deformation of the first deformable membrane causes displacement of the optical fluid and corresponding deformation of the second deformable membrane.

8. The optical device of claim 1, wherein the first and second deformable membranes define opposed optical surfaces of a variable optical element.

9. The optical device of claim 1, wherein the support structure maintains peripheral portions of the first and second deformable membranes in fixed relation while permitting central portions thereof to deform.

10. The optical device of claim 1, wherein the applied voltage controls at least one of optical power, focal length, wavefront profile, astigmatism, spherical aberration, coma, or prism of the optical device.

counterfactuals.output:
## Technical Description: Optical Image Stabilization Device with Fluid-Coupled Deformable Membranes

### Technical Field

The present disclosure relates to optical devices and, more particularly, to an optical image stabilization device suitable for use in imaging systems such as camera modules, mobile electronic devices, endoscopes, machine-vision cameras, wearable devices, and optical sensing systems. The device stabilizes an image by controllably deforming fluid-coupled optical membranes using first and second actuation devices operated relative to a rest position.

### Background

Optical image stabilization is commonly used to reduce image blur caused by motion of an imaging device during exposure or image acquisition. Conventional stabilization systems may employ mechanical translation of a lens group, tilting of an optical element, or sensor-shift mechanisms. Such systems may require relatively large moving masses, complex suspension structures, and significant power consumption, which can be undesirable in compact camera modules.

Fluidic optical elements can provide variable optical properties by deforming one or more transparent membranes in contact with an optical fluid. By controlling the membrane shape, the optical path of incident light may be altered without translating a rigid lens assembly. However, precise stabilization requires controlled and repeatable deformation, preferably with low hysteresis and a well-defined neutral state.

### Summary

An optical device is provided that includes a fluid chamber containing an optically transparent fluid and bounded at least in part by first and second deformable membranes. The first and second deformable membranes are fluid-coupled such that deformation of one membrane produces a pressure or volume change transmitted through the fluid to the other membrane. First and second actuation devices are respectively arranged to act on the first and second deformable membranes. Each actuation device is operable from a rest position to deform the associated membrane in a controlled manner.

The first and second actuation devices may be driven independently or cooperatively to produce a controlled optical wavefront modification, beam deflection, focal adjustment, or a combination thereof. In one implementation, the actuation devices are driven differentially to tilt or laterally shift an effective optical axis of the device, thereby compensating for angular or translational movement of an imaging system. In another implementation, the actuation devices are driven in a coordinated manner to maintain optical power while providing image stabilization.

### General Structure

The optical device may comprise:

1. **A housing or support body** defining an optical aperture and providing mechanical support for the fluidic optical structure.

2. **A fluid chamber** disposed along an optical axis and filled with an optically transparent fluid, such as silicone oil, hydrocarbon oil, aqueous fluid, fluorinated liquid, gel, or other suitable optical medium.

3. **A first deformable membrane** arranged on a first side of the fluid chamber.

4. **A second deformable membrane** arranged on a second side of the fluid chamber, opposite or offset from the first membrane.

5. **A first actuation device** configured to deform the first membrane from a first rest position.

6. **A second actuation device** configured to deform the second membrane from a second rest position.

7. **A control circuit** configured to drive the first and second actuation devices in response to stabilization commands, motion sensor signals, image sensor feedback, or a combination thereof.

The deformable membranes may be optically transparent and may form part of the optical path. The membranes may comprise elastomeric polymer films, transparent silicone membranes, polyurethane films, parylene layers, glass-polymer composite membranes, or other deformable optical materials.

### Fluid-Coupled Membrane Operation

The first and second deformable membranes are coupled by the fluid contained in the chamber. Because the fluid is substantially incompressible, displacement of one membrane changes the pressure distribution within the chamber and influences the shape or position of the other membrane. This fluid coupling allows the optical element to be controlled with high sensitivity and enables the two membranes to operate as a coordinated deformable optical pair.

In a rest state, the first and second actuation devices are in respective rest positions. In the rest state, the membranes may have predetermined shapes, such as planar, convex, concave, or weakly curved profiles. The rest state may correspond to a nominal optical condition, for example zero stabilization correction, a neutral beam direction, or a predetermined focal length.

When stabilization is required, the first actuation device is moved from its rest position to apply force, displacement, pressure, or strain to the first membrane. The second actuation device is likewise moved from its rest position to apply force, displacement, pressure, or strain to the second membrane. The combined membrane deformation modifies the optical path through the fluid chamber so that light exiting the device is redirected or corrected in a manner that counteracts detected motion.

### Actuation Devices

The first and second actuation devices may be selected from various actuator technologies, including but not limited to:

- voice-coil actuators;
- piezoelectric actuators;
- electrostatic actuators;
- electromagnetic actuators;
- shape-memory alloy actuators;
- thermal bimorph actuators;
- dielectric elastomer actuators;
- MEMS actuators;
- hydraulic or pneumatic microactuators;
- mechanical lever or cam-driven actuators.

Each actuation device may include an actuator member, such as a ring, pad, plunger, frame, electrode, or contact structure, arranged to engage a peripheral or central portion of the corresponding membrane. In some embodiments, the actuator member may deform the membrane directly. In other embodiments, the actuator member may deform a membrane support, an intermediate flexible wall, or a pressure-transmitting member coupled to the membrane.

The first actuation device and the second actuation device may be disposed symmetrically with respect to the optical axis, or may be offset to provide directional stabilization. Each actuation device may be configured to operate bidirectionally about its rest position or unidirectionally from the rest position against a restoring force provided by membrane elasticity, fluid pressure, a spring, or a resilient support.

### Rest Position and Neutral Optical State

The rest position of each actuation device may be mechanically defined by a stop, suspension equilibrium, spring preload, magnetic centering force, electrostatic bias, or control-loop reference. The rest positions may correspond to a state in which the membranes are not actively deformed by the actuation devices or are subject only to a predetermined preload.

Operating the actuation devices from the rest position provides a repeatable reference for stabilization control. The control circuit may store calibration data that relates actuator displacement or drive current to membrane shape and optical correction. During operation, the first and second actuation devices may be displaced from their rest positions by respective amounts determined according to detected motion.

In some embodiments, both actuation devices are biased toward the rest position, and stabilization is performed by selectively moving one or both actuation devices away from rest. In other embodiments, the rest position is an intermediate position, allowing positive and negative correction by movement in opposite directions.

### Optical Image Stabilization Function

The device may be positioned in an optical path between an object scene and an image sensor. Motion of the imaging system may be detected using a gyroscope, accelerometer, image-based motion estimator, or other motion detection means. A controller may calculate a desired optical correction corresponding to the detected motion.

The controller then drives the first and second actuation devices such that deformation of the fluid-coupled membranes changes the propagation direction of light passing through the device. For example:

- If the camera rotates upward, the membranes may be deformed to deflect the light downward relative to the image sensor.
- If the camera rotates to the left, the membranes may be deformed to deflect the light to the right.
- If both angular and focus disturbances are present, the actuation devices may be driven to provide combined beam steering and focus correction.

The first and second membranes may be deformed to create an asymmetric optical surface profile. The asymmetric profile may act as a variable prism, thereby shifting the image on the sensor to compensate for motion. Alternatively, the membranes may be deformed in a manner that changes the curvature distribution of the optical surfaces while maintaining a desired focal power.

### Differential and Common-Mode Control

The control system may operate the first and second actuation devices in differential and common-mode control schemes.

In a **differential mode**, the first actuation device is driven in a first direction or by a first amount while the second actuation device is driven in an opposite direction or by a different amount. Differential deformation may generate a wedge-like optical path or a tilted wavefront, resulting in beam steering for image stabilization.

In a **common-mode**, the first and second actuation devices are driven similarly to change the curvature of both membranes or to adjust the internal pressure of the fluid chamber. Common-mode operation may be used to compensate for focus changes, thermal expansion of the fluid, manufacturing tolerances, or optical aberrations.

The controller may combine differential and common-mode signals so that image stabilization is achieved while maintaining a desired focal length or minimizing aberration.

### Example Embodiment

In one embodiment, the optical device includes a cylindrical housing having a central optical aperture. A transparent first membrane is sealed to a first annular support on a front side of the housing, and a transparent second membrane is sealed to a second annular support on a rear side of the housing. The region between the membranes is filled with a transparent optical fluid.

A first annular actuator is arranged adjacent to the first membrane and has a movable portion configured to press on or pull the first membrane at one or more circumferential locations. A second annular actuator is arranged adjacent to the second membrane and has a movable portion configured to press on or pull the second membrane at one or more circumferential locations.

The first and second actuators are each held in a rest position when no stabilization correction is applied. When a motion signal indicates that the optical device has moved, a control circuit applies drive signals to the actuators. The first actuator displaces a selected region of the first membrane, and the second actuator displaces a selected region of the second membrane. The resulting pressure distribution within the optical fluid causes coordinated membrane deformation. Light passing through the device is refracted by the deformed membranes and fluid, thereby shifting the image on an image sensor in a direction opposite to the detected motion.

### Multi-Axis Stabilization

For two-axis stabilization, each actuation device may include a plurality of actuator segments arranged around the optical aperture. For example, four actuator segments may be positioned at top, bottom, left, and right locations. By driving opposing segments differentially, the device may provide stabilization along horizontal and vertical axes.

The first actuation device may include first-axis and second-axis actuator portions, and the second actuation device may include corresponding actuator portions. A controller may independently control these portions to generate membrane deformation patterns corresponding to pitch and yaw compensation. Additional actuator segments may be used to correct roll, higher-order aberrations, or non-linear optical errors.

### Materials and Manufacturing

The housing may be formed from metal, ceramic, glass, silicon, polymer, or composite material. The membranes may be bonded, clamped, welded, or adhesively sealed to the housing to provide a fluid-tight chamber. The optical fluid may be selected to have a refractive index compatible with the membranes and adjacent optical components.

The device may include compensation structures to accommodate thermal expansion of the fluid, such as a compliant reservoir, expansion membrane, or pressure relief volume. Surface coatings may be applied to the membranes to reduce reflection, improve scratch resistance, control wetting, or prevent fluid permeation.

### Sensors and Feedback Control

The optical device may include position sensors, pressure sensors, capacitive sensors, optical sensors, strain gauges, or magnetic sensors configured to detect the position of one or more actuation members or the shape of one or more membranes. Feedback signals from these sensors may be used to regulate the actuation devices and improve stabilization accuracy.

The controller may implement closed-loop control using sensor feedback and motion data. Calibration tables may compensate for non-linear membrane behavior, fluid viscosity, temperature dependence, and actuator hysteresis. The controller may also return the actuation devices to the rest position when stabilization is disabled or when the imaging system enters a low-power state.

### Advantages

The described optical device may provide one or more of the following advantages:

- image stabilization without translating a heavy lens group;
- compact construction suitable for small camera modules;
- reduced mechanical complexity compared with conventional lens-shift systems;
- fast optical correction using low-mass deformable membranes;
- ability to provide beam steering, focus adjustment, or aberration correction;
- repeatable operation due to defined actuator rest positions;
- improved stabilization accuracy through fluid coupling of two deformable membranes;
- potential reduction in power consumption and acoustic noise.

### Industrial Applicability

The optical device may be incorporated into digital cameras, mobile phones, tablet computers, augmented-reality devices, virtual-reality devices, drones, vehicle cameras, medical imaging instruments, surveillance systems, robotic vision systems, and other optical systems requiring compact and efficient image stabilization.

The device is particularly suitable for applications in which space constraints, power consumption, and mechanical robustness are significant design considerations.

## Invention Disclosure: Variable Optical Element with Dual Deformable Membranes

### Title  
Variable optical element using two anchored deformable membranes and constant-volume fluid actuation.

### Field  
The invention relates to adaptive optics, tunable lenses, beam-shaping elements, and variable optical components for imaging, illumination, sensing, and display systems.

### Summary  
A variable optical element comprises two deformable, optically transmissive membranes anchored to a common support structure and enclosing a fixed, substantially incompressible volume of transparent fluid. Each membrane is divided into, or associated with, multiple controllable actuation regions. Control circuitry applies actuation voltages to selected regions of one or both membranes to locally deform the membranes. Because the fluid volume between the membranes remains constant, deformation of one membrane causes corresponding fluid redistribution and coupled deformation of the opposite membrane. By independently controlling actuation voltages across different membrane regions, the optical power, aberration profile, prism angle, cylindrical power, or freeform wavefront shape of the element can be dynamically varied.

### Structure  
The optical element includes:

1. **First deformable membrane** anchored around its perimeter to a frame.  
2. **Second deformable membrane** similarly anchored and spaced from the first membrane.  
3. **Sealed chamber** between the membranes containing a constant volume of optical fluid.  
4. **Actuation electrodes or force-generating regions** associated with different portions of at least one membrane.  
5. **Control means**, such as drive electronics, configured to apply different voltages to different membrane regions.

The membranes may be transparent polymer films, elastomeric layers, glass-supported films, or dielectric elastomer membranes. The fluid may be a transparent oil, gel, aqueous solution, or other optical medium selected for refractive index, viscosity, and stability.

### Operation  
When voltage is applied to a selected actuation region, electrostatic, piezoelectric, dielectric elastomer, electro-wetting, or other electrically induced forces deform the corresponding membrane portion. Since the chamber volume is fixed, displaced fluid redistributes within the chamber, producing a complementary deformation of the other membrane and/or other regions of the same membrane. Spatially varying voltages create spatially varying membrane curvature, allowing the device to function as a tunable lens or adaptive optical surface.

### Advantages  
The dual-membrane, constant-volume configuration provides:

- Wide tunable optical power without changing fluid quantity.  
- Reduced need for pumps or reservoirs.  
- Bidirectional or balanced optical surface control.  
- Ability to generate spherical, cylindrical, prismatic, or higher-order/freeform optical profiles.  
- Compact, low-mass adaptive optical element suitable for integration into miniature optical systems.

### Example Applications  
The invention may be used in autofocus cameras, ophthalmic lenses, augmented-reality optics, endoscopes, microscopes, laser beam steering, wavefront correction, variable focus illumination, and adaptive imaging systems.

### Representative Claim Concept  
A variable optical element comprising first and second anchored deformable membranes defining a sealed chamber containing a substantially constant volume of transparent fluid, and control circuitry configured to apply actuation voltages to different regions of at least one membrane to produce controlled deformation of the membranes and thereby vary an optical property of the element.
